evidence: src/application/order-service.ts: the constructor receives ProductRepository and OrderRepository interfaces, so the service never touches storage directly
placeOrder checks stock on every line before calling products[index].reserve and this.orders.save, keeping the multi-product operation all-or-nothing
progressOrder and cancelOrder hand the state changes to order.advanceTo, order.cancel and product.release

parsedVerdict.reasoning: OrderService acts as an application-layer use-case coordinator. It reaches storage only through the injected ProductRepository and OrderRepository interfaces, never directly. It builds domain objects and hands state changes to domain methods (advanceTo, cancel, reserve, release). It saves results through the repositories and raises DomainError. The file contains no persistence, HTTP or other transport code, and no framework logic. The check in placeOrder that every line has enough stock before any reservation is made fits the application layer, because it keeps the multi-product operation all-or-nothing. normaliseItems checks untrusted input, which is a typical application-layer job. It also merges duplicate lines and enforces "at least one item, positive integer quantity". That is borderline: these could be treated as Order invariants that belong in the domain. They also work fine as input rules for the use case, and the rubric's clear failure cases (infrastructure code in the domain, or business rules in infrastructure or presentation) do not apply. Treating the use of randomUUID as the default ID generator as a dependency issue is out of scope.
